doc.title: Harold Danko interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 28, 2021

title: Army band at Fort Wadsworth and learning woodwind repair
summary: He was drafted in 1969, got into a Staten Island fort band, and learned woodwind repair with Saul Fromkin, which later helped with Woody Herman's horn.

blocks.x: not getting a teaching gig, and I got my draft notice right away, in 1969. So but I auditioned in Indianapolis, figuring that’s close enough to Ohio, maybe I can hang in there, you know a six hour drive and whatever. And the guy in Indianapolis was very great. He had me sit in, the audition was sitting in with his big band. And he said, “You play too well, you don’t want to come and be in a fort band.” He said, “the only thing the Army can offer you is a location.” I went hmm okay. He said if you ever want to go to Europe, want to travel someplace, and I said, “Is there any place in New York?” “Oh yeah there are bands in New York.” So he made a call to a Staten Island band, it was a fort band located in Staten Island. They said they had openings. They had actually, the officers really weren’t running it, it was like an enlisted guy that answered the phone. They already had like four or five piano players. But he said yes so I got a chance to go to Fort Wadsworth in Staten Island. And after Basic Training, and kind of, get into this band, that already had piano players. And great, really wonderful musicians at that time. So that was a kind of a continuation of my education. Near the end of my Army career another option came about when, because at the end of the, it was 1972 and there was a lot of, you know that anti-war thing, whatever that was going on, and the people that were getting out of the Army, the Army was suddenly allotting money to train people in a trade. So I said oh wow, piano tuning. Maybe I can get a piano tuner, or whatever. So there was a thing where they said, “Well you already have a degree in whatever, in music.” I said, “I’ve got to get into a trade.” So I went on the lookout for a piano tuner and then there was somebody that had done woodwind repair with Saul Fromkin in New York. He was a woodwind repairman that was very well known. And so I called Saul asking if he knew any piano tuners that I could — and he said, “Oh you should do woodwind repair.” Of course he’s going to get some money from the Army to train me. And I said, “Well I don’t really play the woodwinds.” He said, “It’s better, it’s like you’ll be scientific” or whatever. So I went in and I learned how to repair woodwinds. I was pretty awful at it. I was very slow. But Saul entrusted me to repair some student metal clarinets every now and then. And once he gave me an open holed flute, uh, which took me forever to re-pad. But anyway I had some skill going there, which actually served me well in Woody Herman because Tom Anastas who as the baritone player used to warm up Woody’s horn and there was something wrong. I don’t know what Tom might have done with the horn but there was one time where it got a little bit out of line and I was able to look at it enough and get it so Woody would know there was something wrong but it wasn’t horrible, like that anyone had thrown it or anything. But when I got back to New York there was the idea that maybe I would do this, you know this woodwind repair thing in addition to trying to make my way.
